q: Which glass shape best serves a fine Champagne at table?
opts: A wide, shallow coupe with a broad open rim
A narrow, straight-sided flute with no bowl at all
A small fortified-wine glass, filled to the brim
A tulip that swells at the bowl and narrows at the rim
exp: The bowl gives the aroma room to gather and the narrowed rim delivers it. A coupe spills both the aroma and the bubbles away, whatever its history at parties.

q: A bottle needs chilling quickly during service. Which is fastest?
opts: The freezer compartment for twenty minutes
A bucket of half ice and half water
The main refrigerator at four degrees
exp: Water carries heat away from the entire surface of the bottle where ice alone touches it only at points. A handful of salt lowers the bath temperature further still.

q: A freshly polished glass kills the bead within seconds of pouring. What is the usual cause?
opts: Detergent residue left in the bowl
exp: Surfactants collapse foam on contact. Rinse with hot water and polish over steam with a clean, unscented linen cloth, never with a soapy one.

q: Every classic route to a naturally sweet wine works on one of two variables. Which pair?
opts: Concentrating the sugar in the grape, or halting the ferment early
Extending skin contact, or extending lees ageing
Lowering the acidity of the must, or raising the alcohol
Adding sugar to the must, or adding sugar to the finished wine
exp: Noble rot, frost and drying all take water out of the berry, so what remains is more concentrated. Halting the ferment early leaves behind sugar the yeast never used up, and fortification is the blunt version of that: spirit added partway through kills the yeast while grape sugar is still in the vat.

q: Each German Pradikat level carries a minimum juice sugar, read on a scale named after a nineteenth-century Pforzheim goldsmith. Which scale?
exp: Oechsle measures the density of the must, so a reading of 150 means a litre of juice weighs 150 grams more than a litre of water. Brix, Baume and the Austrian KMW scale record the same ripeness on different arithmetic.

q: A technical sheet for a dessert wine gives 120 grams per litre alongside the alcohol and the total acidity. Which measurement is that?
exp: Residual sugar is what the yeast never converted, and dessert styles run from roughly 45 grams per litre to several hundred. The other three are reported in the same units but at a small fraction of that figure.

q: Two dessert wines carry an identical 150 grams of residual sugar, yet one tastes fresh and the other cloying. Which component most often accounts for the difference?
exp: Sugar with nothing to cut it turns syrupy in the mouth and tiring after half a glass. It is why the great sweet wines come from cool sites and high-acid grapes such as Riesling, Chenin Blanc and Furmint.

q: Chateau d'Yquem is often said to make about a glass of wine from each vine. What lies behind a figure that low?
opts: The appellation forbids more than one bunch to be left on each vine
The greater part of the crop is sold off in bulk to negociants
Most of the volume is lost to evaporation during long barrel ageing
Shrivelled berries hold little juice, and pickers reject much of it
exp: A berry that has given up half its water yields half as much juice, and fruit that has not rotted cleanly is left on the vine or declassified as the pickers work through the rows again and again. The tiny yield is a consequence of the method rather than a rule imposed on it.

q: German producers may sweeten a finished dry wine by blending back unfermented juice held aside from the same harvest. What is that reserve called?
exp: Sussreserve is grape juice rather than sugar, so sweetness and wine come from the same fruit. It is legal at every German quality level, Pradikat wines included, so long as the juice is unchaptalised and of at least equal quality from the same region, though the finest sweet wines still get their sugar from a fermentation that stopped of its own accord.

q: A grey fungus punctures the skin of a ripe white grape and, given the right weather, transforms it. What is its Latin name?
exp: One organism causes both noble rot and the grey rot that ruins a crop, and only the weather decides which. The others are downy mildew, powdery mildew and black rot, none of which ever does a grower a favour.

q: Misty, damp mornings give way to dry breezy afternoons right through the autumn. Why does that alternation matter to a sweet-wine grower?
opts: Humidity lets noble rot take hold, and the dry afternoons check it
Damp air prevents the fungus from establishing at all
Humidity raises the sugar while the dry afternoons raise the acidity
The daily temperature swing is what sets the colour of the fruit
exp: Unbroken damp turns the same fungus into grey rot, which splits berries, taints flavour and can take a crop in days. The dry afternoon checks its spread and lets the punctured fruit dehydrate instead.

q: Rain that never lets up through the harvest turns the sweet-wine grower's ally into a disaster. What is that ruinous form called?
exp: Grey rot is the same species behaving badly, spreading through sound fruit and leaving mouldy, tainted juice. Sour rot is a separate affair involving bacteria, wild yeasts and fruit flies.

q: Fungal threads pierce the skin and the berry shrivels over the following days. What is actually happening inside it?
opts: Alcohol begins to form inside the intact grape
The berry draws water up from the vine and swells until the skin splits
The fungus manufactures sugar and feeds it into the berry
Water escapes through the perforated skin, concentrating what remains
exp: No sugar is added from outside the berry. The fungus opens thousands of tiny holes, the berry loses water to the air, and everything dissolved in that water is left behind in a much smaller volume, minus the share of sugar and acid the fungus takes for itself.

q: Botrytised wines feel unusually viscous in the mouth at only moderate alcohol. Which compound generated by the fungus helps explain that?
exp: The fungus produces glycerol as it works through the grape's sugar, and it survives fermentation into the bottle. Texture in these wines comes from sugar, glycerol and extract together rather than from alcohol.

q: Honey, beeswax, dried apricot, marmalade and a faint mushroomy note run through a deep golden wine. Which process produced that set of aromas?
opts: Ageing under a veil of yeast
exp: Those markers belong to the fungus rather than to the grape, which is why a botrytised Semillon and a botrytised Furmint smell more like each other than either does like its own dry version.

q: Juice pressed from nobly rotten fruit browns alarmingly fast and shrugs off the usual dose of sulphur. Which enzyme carried by the fungus is responsible?
exp: Laccase is an oxidase the fungus brings with it, and unlike the grape's own oxidase it is barely troubled by sulphur dioxide. Cellars handling botrytised must work quickly and keep air away from it.
